title: Long Mott (Dow / X-energy): 2026/09/19 - Comment (1) E-mail regarding LMGS CP Hearing [['General FR Notice Comment Letter']]

documents.text:
From:                   wilsonalamobay@aol.com
Sent:                   Saturday, September 19, 2026 1:07 PM
To:                     LMGS-CPHearing Resource
Subject:                [External_Sender] Formal Public Comment: Opposition to the Environmental
                        Assessment and Demand for a Full EIS for the Long Mott Gernerating Station
                        (Docket No. PROJ-0961

To: LMGS-CPHearing@nrc.gov
Cc: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission Staff

To Whom It May Concern,

I am a local fourth generation fisher woman from Seadrift, Texas. My family has lived and
fished in this area for over 100 years. This Long Mott Generating Station project that is
being proposed will be right outside my hometown of Seadrift and near our home bays of
San Antonio, Mission, and Guadalupe Bays. I am writing to formally register my opposition
to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s (NRC) Environmental Assessment (EA) and
its associated Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) for the proposed Long Mott
Generating Station (LMGS) in Calhoun County, Texas.

Bypassing a full Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) for a first-of-a-kind commercial
nuclear deployment on the Texas Gulf Coast is legally and environmentally indefensible. I
urge the NRC to halt this expedited review process and mandate a comprehensive, multi-
year EIS based on the following critical deficiencies in the existing project documents:

1. Severe Safety Risks Due to the Lack of a Traditional Structural Containment Dome
The Xe-100 pebble-bed design proposed for this site lacks a traditional, thick, steel-
reinforced high-pressure concrete containment dome. The applicant relies instead on a
theoretical concept of "functional containment" embedded inside the fuel pellets
themselves. While this might suffice in low-risk interior regions, it represents an
unacceptable point of failure on a hurricane frontline. The project documents do not prove
that a standard industrial building lacking a traditional heavy containment dome can
survive the impact of extreme, wind-borne tornado and hurricane debris, or catastrophic
storm surges, without risking an unmitigated atmospheric release of radiation.

2. Unjustified Elimination of the Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ) and Public Health
Risks
The applicant is using the unproven nature of the Xe-100 design to ask for a near-total
exemption from traditional 10-mile Emergency Planning Zones (EPZs), attempting to shrink
the evacuation boundary to the facility's fence line. This is a severe threat to public health.
The NRC cannot ignore a landmark nationwide study published in February 2026 by the
Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, which revealed that residential proximity to
operational U.S. nuclear plants is associated with a measurable, significant increase in
cancer mortality rates. Shrinking or eliminating emergency evacuation zones while new
 epidemiological data proves a baseline health risk to surrounding communities constitutes
a severe regulatory failure.

3. Illegal Failure to Consider Cumulative Regional Impacts (The Blue Energy Project)
Under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the NRC is legally required to
evaluate cumulative environmental impacts—the compounding stress of the proposed
facility alongside other reasonably foreseeable projects in the same immediate area. On
September 15, 2026, Blue Energy formally submitted its construction permit application to
the NRC to build up to five small modular nuclear reactors at the nearby Port of Victoria.
Because the NRC isolated the Long Mott project under an expedited EA, it completely
ignored this massive, overlapping regional nuclear development next door. A "Finding of
No Significant Impact" is legally invalid when the NRC is simultaneously planning a
second, multi-reactor nuclear facility in the exact same watershed without analyzing their
joint, compounding toll on our regional infrastructure and environment.

4. Extreme Coastal Vulnerability, Climate Impacts, and Grid Resilience Blind Spots
The project site on the Victoria Barge Canal sits on the front lines of severe Gulf Coast
weather. The current environmental documents fail to adequately model the intensifying
impacts of climate change, including Category 5 hurricanes, catastrophic localized
flooding, and rapid sea-level rise. The EA provides no realistic safety margin for a total
regional grid collapse caused by coastal storms. If a hurricane disrupts the facility’s
backup power and causes the unproven, high-temperature helium cooling loops to break
down, the surrounding community faces a direct risk of public radiation exposure. Local
families must not be treated as a regulatory test case for an unproven reactor
configuration lacking physical containment structures in a severe weather zone.

5. Severe and Compounding Threats to Estuarine Fisheries
The fragile San Antonio Bay system supports local shrimpers, crabbers, fin fishermen, and
oyster harvesters who rely on pristine water quality for their livelihoods. The operational
impacts of the Long Mott facility—specifically thermal pollution from discharging hot
wastewater and water intake systems that trap and destroy marine larvae—will devastate
local nurseries. When combined with the massive cooling water demands of the newly
proposed Blue Energy project nearby, the cumulative destruction of marine life will
permanently damage the local coastal economy.

6. Co-Applicant's Record of Corporate Environmental Non-Compliance
The nuclear facility is scheduled to be co-located at Dow Chemical’s Seadrift Operations.
In February 2026, the State of Texas filed a major enforcement lawsuit against Dow
Chemical, Union Carbide, and Braskem for hundreds of severe water pollution violations
regarding millions of plastic pellets (nurdles) illegally discharged into our watershed.
Concurrently, Dow attempted to evade accountability by asking state regulators to modify
its permits to effectively legalize these discharges. If Dow Chemical cannot safely manage
basic plastic beads without triggering a lawsuit from the Texas Attorney General, they
 cannot be trusted to host high-temperature nuclear fuel. The NRC must not grant nuclear
permits to a corporate host with an active, state-prosecuted record of environmental
negligence.

7. Deficiencies in Financial Qualifications and Decommissioning Assurances
Because Long Mott Energy, LLC is structured as a limited liability company, there are
insufficient legal guarantees protecting local taxpayers. The project documents do not
outline adequate, legally binding financial bonding to cover catastrophic cost overruns,
project abandonment, or eventual radiological decommissioning. If this facility is crippled
by a coastal hurricane or corporate bankruptcy, local residents will be left holding the
financial and environmental burden of a contaminated site.

Conclusion
The combination of an unproven reactor design completely lacking a traditional physical
containment dome, a highly vulnerable coastal location, a massive newly proposed
neighboring nuclear project, and a host applicant facing active state environmental
prosecution legally mandates a rigorous, transparent evaluation. The current
Environmental Assessment is entirely insufficient. I request that the NRC deny the
construction permit under the current expedited track and order a full Environmental
Impact Statement.

Sincerely,

Diane Wilson
600 Ramona Rd.
Seadrift, Texas 77983
361-218-2353
